When shared mutable state is guarded by a mutex that is also needed by latency-sensitive paths (an IPC command handler, a GTK/main-thread event loop, a health-check loop), never perform a blocking operation (I/O, writes, D-Bus/network calls) while holding that lock. Acquire the lock only to read or hand off a cloned handle, release it immediately, and push any blocking work to a dedicated worker (a per-resource thread fed by an unbounded channel, or a detached probe thread with `recv_timeout`) so the critical thread stays responsive even if the blocking call stalls indefinitely.

```rust
// Bad: holds the sessions lock across a blocking write
let mut sessions = state.sessions.lock().unwrap();
sessions.get_mut(&id).unwrap().writer.write_all(data.as_bytes())?;

// Good: enqueue onto a dedicated writer thread, release the lock immediately
let sender = {
    let sessions = state.sessions.lock().unwrap();
    sessions.get(&id).ok_or("no such terminal")?.sender.clone()
};
sender.send(data).map_err(|_| "terminal closed")?;
```

The same discipline applies to probes run from a thread that must not stall (e.g. a main-thread close handler): run the check on a background thread and bound the wait with a timeout, choosing the safe default (e.g. "assume no host" / "keep previous behavior") when the timeout fires, and letting the probe finish on its own rather than blocking the caller.

When multiple mutexes protect related state, document and strictly follow a single lock-acquisition order (e.g. "process before ws_endpoint, never the reverse") everywhere both are touched, including teardown paths, to prevent deadlocks between concurrent callers.

Finally, when a tracked resource (a session, a child process) can be replaced while a background thread is still finishing work on the old one, tag the resource with an id/generation/pid and verify that tag still matches current state before finalizing, removing, or mutating it — otherwise a stale thread can clobber state that already belongs to its successor.
